questions.title: Membrane permeability change during depolarization
questions.question: In nerve fibers, during the depolarization phase of an action potential, the permeability of the membrane:

explanations.A: Incorrect. K+ permeability rises during repolarization, not during the depolarization phase itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Depolarization is caused by a sudden, massive increase in the membrane's permeability to Na+, as voltage-gated Na+ channels open in response to the membrane reaching threshold. Na+ then rushes into the cell down its steep electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane potential rapidly from the resting level through zero to a positive overshoot. This regenerative Na+ influx, feeding further channel opening as the membrane depolarizes, is the defining ionic event of the depolarization phase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ca2+ permeability increases significantly in some cell types (such as cardiac and smooth muscle) but is not the main driver of the nerve fibre action potential's depolarization phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cl- permeability is not what rises sharply during depolarization.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Membrane permeability changes dramatically during depolarization; it is far from unchanged.

questions.learning_objective: State that depolarization is caused by a sharp increase in membrane Na+ permeability.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Ionic Basis of Depolarization

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.12

questions.title: Cause of the after-hyperpolarization phase
questions.question: The after-hyperpolarization phase of the action potential is caused by which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chloride currents are not what drives the after-hyperpolarization phase.
explanations.B: Correct. The after-hyperpolarization (positive after-potential) is caused by a continuing outward potassium current, produced because voltage-gated K+ channels remain open slightly longer than it takes the membrane to return to its resting level. This persisting K+ efflux drives the membrane potential briefly past the resting level, making it transiently more negative (hyperpolarized) before the K+ channels finally close and the potential settles back to rest. This is a direct continuation of the same K+ conductance responsible for repolarization, simply outlasting it slightly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An inward chloride current is not the mechanism of after-hyperpolarization.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium current, when present, is inward (depolarizing), not outward, and Na+ channels are inactivated by this phase in any case.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Outward calcium current is not the basis of after-hyperpolarization in the nerve action potential.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the after-hyperpolarization phase to a persisting outward K+ current from voltage-gated K+ channels that remain open past repolarization.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Hyperpolarization Phase

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.12

questions.title: Ion producing the greatest depolarization
questions.question: The membrane potential will depolarize by the greatest amount if the membrane permeability increases for which of the following ions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Combining Na+ and K+ permeability increases would partly offset each other's opposing effects on membrane potential, producing less depolarization than a Na+ increase alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increasing Cl- permeability tends to hyperpolarize or stabilize the membrane near its resting level, not depolarize it, since the Cl- equilibrium potential is near or below the resting potential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing K+ permeability drives the membrane potential toward the very negative K+ equilibrium potential, hyperpolarizing rather than depolarizing it.
explanations.D: Correct. Because the Na+ equilibrium potential is strongly positive (around +60 mV), increasing membrane permeability to Na+ drives the membrane potential toward that positive value, producing the greatest depolarization of any single-ion permeability increase. This is exactly the mechanism that generates the action potential's depolarization phase: a selective, large increase in Na+ permeability. No other major ion's equilibrium potential is positive enough to depolarize the membrane this strongly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Combining K+ and Cl- permeability increases moves the membrane potential toward negative equilibrium potentials, causing hyperpolarization rather than depolarization.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why increasing Na+ permeability produces the greatest membrane depolarization, based on Na+'s strongly positive equilibrium potential.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Ionic Basis of Depolarization

questions.title: Na+ channel gate open at rest
questions.question: As regards Na+ voltage-gated channels, which gate is open at rest?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The activation (M) gate is closed at rest; it is the inactivation gate that is open at rest.
explanations.B: Correct. The voltage-gated Na+ channel has two gates: an activation gate near the outer surface and an inactivation gate on the inner surface. At the resting membrane potential, the activation gate is closed while the inactivation gate (H gate) is open, so the channel as a whole is in the resting (closed but available) state. Depolarization to threshold opens the activation gate first, letting Na+ flow in; only afterwards does the slower inactivation gate close, ending Na+ entry.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The voltage-gated Na+ channel is described by activation and inactivation gates, not a separate 'N' gate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. One of the two gates (the inactivation/H gate) is indeed open at rest, so the answer is not 'none'.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+ channel's inactivation (H) gate is open and its activation (M) gate is closed at rest.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Sodium Channel Gating

questions.title: Trigger for neuronal firing
questions.question: A neuron fires when which one of the following events occurs?

options.A: Depolarization at the axon hillock exceeds the threshold for excitation
options.B: There is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)
options.C: Hyperpolarization occurs at the axon hillock

explanations.A: Correct. A neuron fires — generates a propagated action potential — specifically when the summed depolarization at the axon hillock reaches or exceeds the threshold for excitation, the voltage at which enough voltage-gated Na+ channels open to make the regenerative depolarizing cycle self-sustaining. Below this threshold, only a local, non-propagated response occurs, no matter how many depolarizing inputs summate. This threshold-crossing at the axon hillock, specifically, is what converts graded synaptic inputs into an all-or-none, propagated impulse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An EPSP is a depolarizing synaptic potential that can contribute toward firing, but by itself, without reaching threshold at the axon hillock, it does not guarantee the neuron fires.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperpolarization moves the membrane potential further from threshold, making firing less, not more, likely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neurotransmitter-receptor binding can initiate a postsynaptic potential, but firing itself requires that potential to summate and cross threshold at the axon hillock.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Opening Cl- channels typically produces an inhibitory (hyperpolarizing or stabilizing) effect, working against firing rather than triggering it.

questions.learning_objective: State that a neuron fires when depolarization at the axon hillock exceeds the threshold for excitation.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Threshold and Firing

questions.title: Mechanism of repolarization
questions.question: About repolarization, which of the following is TRUE?

options.A: Results from closure of sodium gates and opening of potassium gates
options.B: Occurs at first gradual then becomes fast
options.C: Is followed by appearance of the response
options.E: Is represented by the ascending limb of the spike

explanations.A: Correct. Repolarization results from the closure of the (already-inactivating) voltage-gated Na+ channels together with the opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, which had opened more slowly in response to depolarization. As Na+ entry stops and K+ efflux rises, the membrane potential is driven back down from its positive overshoot toward the resting level. This combination of falling Na+ conductance and rising K+ conductance is the defining ionic mechanism of repolarization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Repolarization occurs rapidly for roughly its first 70 percent and then more slowly for the remainder, the reverse of 'gradual then fast'.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Repolarization is itself part of the response (the action potential), not something that precedes and is 'followed by' the response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Repolarization occurs due to K+ efflux (outward movement), not K+ influx.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ascending limb of the spike is the depolarization phase; repolarization is represented by the descending limb.

questions.learning_objective: State that repolarization results from closure of Na+ channels together with opening of K+ channels.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Repolarization Mechanism

questions.title: Cause of the hyperpolarization phase
questions.question: The hyperpolarization phase of the action potential is due to which of the following?

options.A: The opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
options.B: Prolonged opening of voltage-gated K+ channels
options.C: The closure of resting Na+ channels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are inactivated (closed) by this point in the action potential, not opening.
explanations.B: Correct. The hyperpolarization phase is due to the prolonged opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, which stay open slightly longer than the time needed for the membrane to return to its resting level. This extra, persisting K+ efflux carries the membrane potential briefly past the resting level, transiently making the inside more negative than at rest, before the K+ channels finally close. This is the same K+ conductance that drives repolarization, simply outlasting the return to rest.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Resting Na+ channels are not a distinct gate being closed here; Na+ channel inactivation, not resting-channel closure, is what ends Na+ entry earlier in the action potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chloride channel closure is not the basis of the hyperpolarization phase.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chloride channel opening is not the mechanism of after-hyperpolarization in this context.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the hyperpolarization phase to the prolonged opening of voltage-gated K+ channels past the point of full repolarization.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Hyperpolarization Phase

questions.title: Effect of hypokalemia on the resting potential
questions.question: Hypokalemia (decrease in plasma K+ concentration) would be expected to result in:

options.B: A more negative resting membrane potential (RMP)
options.D: Decrease in the firing level of neurons

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the resting potential, which moves it further from threshold and tends to decrease, not increase, excitability.
explanations.B: Correct. By the Nernst equation, the K+ equilibrium potential depends on the ratio of intracellular to extracellular K+ concentration; lowering extracellular K+ (hypokalemia) increases that ratio, making the K+ equilibrium potential — and, because the resting membrane sits close to it, the resting membrane potential itself — more negative than normal. This hyperpolarization moves the membrane further from the threshold needed to fire an action potential. This Nernst-based relationship is why clinically significant hypokalemia disturbs the excitability of nerve and muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because the resting potential is heavily K+-dependent, a change in extracellular K+ concentration does change the RMP, not leave it unchanged.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The threshold (firing level) itself is not directly lowered by hypokalemia; if anything, the larger gap between the more negative RMP and the (relatively unchanged) firing level makes the neuron harder, not easier, to fire.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the Nernst relationship to predict that hypokalemia makes the resting membrane potential more negative.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Applying the Nernst Relationship

questions.title: Duration of the negative after-potential
questions.question: The duration of the negative after-potential of a neuronal action potential is typically:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 5 ms is longer than the typically quoted duration for the negative after-potential.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 25 ms overstates the typically quoted duration of the negative after-potential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 200 ms is far too long for the negative after-potential; that order of magnitude belongs to phenomena such as the cardiac plateau, not the nerve after-potential.
explanations.D: Correct. As taught in this course, the negative after-potential of the neuronal action potential typically lasts about 4 ms, a brief tail following the main spike during which repolarization has not yet fully completed to the resting level. This is distinct from the longer after-hyperpolarization (positive after-potential) that follows it. The short duration reflects how quickly the underlying Na+ and K+ conductance changes resolve once the main spike has passed.

questions.learning_objective: State the typical duration of the negative after-potential as taught in this course.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Phase Durations

questions.title: Channel activation and inactivation during the action potential
questions.question: An action potential in nerve fibers is characterized by which one of the following?

options.A: Includes changes due to channel activation and inactivation
options.D: Is conducted rapidly in C fibers

explanations.A: Correct. The nerve action potential is characterized by sequential changes in voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channel states — activation (opening) and inactivation (closing) — that together produce depolarization, repolarization and the refractory period. The Na+ channel's own activation followed by inactivation, and the K+ channel's slower activation, together account for the entire shape of the spike. This is fundamentally different from a channel that is simply passively open or closed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Unlike a subthreshold local response, the action potential is a propagated, all-or-none event, not confined to the site of stimulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The action potential depends mainly on voltage-gated channels actively opening and closing, not on passive (leak) channels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C fibers are unmyelinated and among the slowest-conducting fibre types, not rapidly conducting.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The axonal action potential depends mainly on voltage-gated channels, not ligand-gated (chemically activated) channels, which instead mediate synaptic transmission.

questions.learning_objective: State that the action potential is characterized by voltage-gated channel activation and inactivation, not passive or ligand-gated conduction.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Sodium Channel Gating

questions.title: What terminates the action potential
questions.question: The action potential of a neuron is characterized by which one of the following?

options.A: Declines in amplitude as it moves along the axon
options.B: Is initiated by efflux of Na+ ions
options.C: Is not associated with excitability changes in the axon
options.D: Is not associated with movement of Na+ or K+ across the cell membrane
options.E: Is terminated by efflux of K+ ions

explanations.A: Incorrect. By the all-or-none law, a propagated action potential does not decline in amplitude as it travels along the axon; each segment regenerates the full-sized spike.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The action potential is initiated by influx, not efflux, of Na+ ions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The action potential is directly associated with excitability changes — increased excitability during initial depolarization, followed by the absolute and relative refractory periods.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The action potential is fundamentally the result of Na+ and K+ movement across the membrane; it is not independent of it.
explanations.E: Correct. The action potential is terminated — brought back down from its peak toward the resting level — by the efflux of K+ ions through voltage-gated K+ channels, which open in response to depolarization. As Na+ channels inactivate and K+ channels open, K+ leaves the cell down its electrochemical gradient, repolarizing the membrane and ending the spike. This K+ efflux is the direct ionic basis of both repolarization and, if it persists slightly longer, the hyperpolarization that follows.

questions.learning_objective: State that the action potential is terminated by K+ efflux through voltage-gated K+ channels.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Repolarization Mechanism

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.14

questions.title: K+ channel opening and repolarization
questions.question: The opening of axon membrane voltage-gated potassium channels is responsible for which part of the action potential?

options.A: Contraction of the post-synaptic muscle fiber

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscle fibre contraction is a downstream effect of neuromuscular transmission, not a direct consequence of axonal K+ channel opening.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Depolarization is driven by Na+ channel opening (Na+ influx), not K+ channel opening.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The overshoot is the peak positive excursion of the spike, produced by the Na+-driven depolarization, not by K+ channel opening.
explanations.D: Correct. Voltage-gated K+ channels open in response to depolarization, somewhat more slowly than Na+ channels, and the resulting outward K+ current drives the membrane potential back down from its positive overshoot toward the resting level. This K+-efflux-driven return toward rest is, by definition, the repolarization phase of the action potential. Its slower onset relative to Na+ channel opening is exactly why depolarization precedes repolarization in the sequence of the spike.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neurotransmitter vesicular release at the synaptic terminal is triggered by Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels there, not by axonal K+ channel opening.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute repolarization of the membrane specifically to the opening of voltage-gated K+ channels.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Repolarization Mechanism

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.15

questions.title: Ionic basis of depolarization (permeability)
questions.question: Depolarization:

options.A: Is associated with an increase in membrane permeability to Na+
options.B: Is terminated with closure of voltage-activated K+ channels

explanations.A: Correct. Depolarization is directly associated with a sharp increase in membrane permeability to Na+, as voltage-gated Na+ channels open once the membrane reaches threshold. The resulting Na+ influx drives the membrane potential from the resting level through zero to a positive overshoot, and this rising Na+ permeability is regenerative, opening still more channels as depolarization proceeds. It is this specific ionic permeability change that defines the depolarization phase of the action potential.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Depolarization is terminated by inactivation of Na+ channels and opening of K+ channels, not by closure of K+ channels, which instead terminates repolarization/hyperpolarization.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Depolarization is followed, at the neuromuscular junction and in the muscle fibre, by excitation-contraction coupling and contraction, not relaxation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. K+ efflux causes repolarization, not depolarization.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ca2+ efflux is not the cause of depolarization; where Ca2+ is involved (as at presynaptic terminals), it is Ca2+ influx that matters.

questions.learning_objective: State that depolarization is associated with a sharp increase in membrane Na+ permeability.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Ionic Basis of Depolarization

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.15

questions.title: Repolarization driven by K+ efflux
questions.question: Repolarization:

options.A: Occurs at first gradually then becomes fast
options.C: Is represented by the ascending limb of the spike
options.D: Means the first phase of the action potential

explanations.A: Incorrect. Repolarization occurs rapidly at first, for roughly its first 70 percent, and then more slowly for the rest — the reverse of gradual-then-fast.
explanations.B: Correct. Repolarization occurs because voltage-gated K+ channels, which opened in response to depolarization, drive a sustained outward K+ current once Na+ channels have inactivated and stopped further Na+ entry. This net K+ efflux carries positive charge out of the cell, returning the membrane potential from its positive overshoot back toward the negative resting level. K+ efflux, not any change in Na+ movement, is the specific ionic event that defines repolarization.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ascending limb of the spike is depolarization; repolarization corresponds to the descending limb.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Repolarization is not the first phase of the action potential; depolarization precedes it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Repolarization requires Na+ channels to be inactivated (closed), not opened; K+ channel opening drives repolarization instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that repolarization occurs due to K+ efflux through voltage-gated K+ channels.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Repolarization Mechanism

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.15

questions.title: Full ionic mechanism of repolarization
questions.question: Repolarization:

options.A: Occurs at first gradually then becomes fast
options.B: Is due to stoppage of Na+ influx and the beginning of K+ efflux
options.C: Is followed by appearance of the response
options.D: Represents the ascending limb of the spike

explanations.A: Incorrect. Repolarization occurs rapidly at first and then more slowly, the reverse of gradual-then-fast.
explanations.B: Correct. Repolarization results from two simultaneous ionic events: the stoppage of Na+ influx, as voltage-gated Na+ channels inactivate, and the beginning (and continuation) of K+ efflux, as voltage-gated K+ channels open. Neither event alone fully explains repolarization — it is the combination of falling Na+ conductance and rising K+ conductance that reverses the depolarizing trend and returns the membrane potential toward rest. This two-part mechanism is the complete ionic basis of the repolarization phase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Repolarization is itself part of the action potential response, not something that precedes and is 'followed by' the response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ascending limb of the spike represents depolarization; repolarization is the descending limb.

questions.learning_objective: State that repolarization requires both the stoppage of Na+ influx and the onset of K+ efflux.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Repolarization Mechanism

questions.title: Amplitude of the nerve action potential
questions.question: The amplitude of the action potential is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 35 mV is close to the overshoot value alone (the positive peak above zero), not the total spike amplitude measured from the resting level.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 20 mV is too small to represent the full spike amplitude from resting potential to overshoot.
explanations.C: Correct. The amplitude of the action potential is the total voltage swing from the resting membrane potential to the peak of the overshoot. Starting from a resting potential of about -70 mV and rising to an overshoot of about +35 mV gives a total swing of roughly 105 mV. This full excursion, not just the positive overshoot alone, is what is meant by the amplitude of the spike.
explanations.D: Incorrect. -70 mV is the resting membrane potential itself, not the amplitude (total swing) of the action potential.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate the amplitude of the action potential as the total swing from resting potential to overshoot.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Spike Amplitude

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.15

questions.title: Na+ channel opening during depolarization
questions.question: During depolarization:

options.C: The membrane becomes impermeable to Na+
options.D: When the membrane potential reaches -55 mV, Na+ and K+ channels open at the same time

explanations.A: Correct. Depolarization occurs because voltage-gated Na+ channels open once the membrane reaches threshold, letting Na+ rush into the cell down its electrochemical gradient. This Na+ influx is regenerative: the resulting depolarization opens still more Na+ channels, driving the membrane potential rapidly toward the Na+ equilibrium potential. The opening of these channels is the specific, defining event of the depolarization phase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. K+ efflux is the hallmark of repolarization, driven by the slower-opening K+ channels, not of depolarization itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Depolarization is caused by a sharp increase, not a decrease, in membrane permeability to Na+.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Na+ and K+ channels do not open at exactly the same time; Na+ channels open first and more rapidly at threshold, while K+ channels open somewhat later and more slowly, which is exactly why depolarization precedes repolarization.

questions.learning_objective: State that Na+ channels open during depolarization, ahead of the slower-opening K+ channels.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Ionic Basis of Depolarization

questions.title: General properties of the nerve impulse
questions.question: About the nerve impulse, which of the following is TRUE?

options.A: Maximum conduction is one meter per second
options.B: It can travel in one direction only
options.C: It is conducted at the same speed in different axons
options.E: It is not delayed at synapses before transmission

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conduction velocity in large, myelinated fibres can reach well over 100 metres per second, far above one metre per second.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An axon can conduct in either direction from its point of stimulation; only in vivo, because of one-way conduction through synapses, does the impulse normally travel in one direction (orthodromic) once it reaches a synapse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conduction speed varies considerably between axons, depending on fibre diameter and myelination (A, B and C fibre classes each conduct at markedly different velocities).
explanations.D: Correct. Propagating a nerve impulse requires metabolic energy, because the Na+-K+ pump must continuously use ATP to restore the ionic gradients run down by each action potential's Na+ influx and K+ efflux. Without this ongoing, energy-dependent pump activity, the Na+ and K+ gradients that make each subsequent impulse possible would gradually dissipate. This dependence on active transport is why nerve conduction is an energy-requiring process, not a purely passive one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Synaptic transmission does introduce a measurable delay (synaptic delay) before the impulse continues into the next neuron, so the impulse is delayed at synapses.

questions.learning_objective: State that nerve impulse conduction requires energy, supplied by the ATP-dependent Na+-K+ pump restoring ionic gradients.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Energy Cost of Nerve Conduction

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.16

questions.title: Membrane voltage that activates voltage-gated Na+ channels
questions.question: Which membrane voltage activates the neuronal voltage-gated Na+ channels?

explanations.A: Incorrect. -70 mV is the typical resting membrane potential itself, not the threshold voltage that opens voltage-gated Na+ channels.
explanations.B: Correct. As taught in this course, a membrane potential of about -55 mV is the threshold voltage at which enough voltage-gated Na+ channels open (their activation gates open) to make the depolarizing Na+ influx regenerative and self-sustaining. Below this threshold, any Na+ channels that open do not trigger enough further opening to produce a full, propagated action potential — only a local, subthreshold response occurs. Reaching this threshold voltage is what converts a graded depolarizing stimulus into an all-or-none spike.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0 mV is passed through during the rising phase of the spike, well after Na+ channels have already opened at threshold, not the voltage that opens them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A positive 50 mV is near the peak of the overshoot, not the threshold voltage for channel activation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A positive 35 mV is close to the overshoot peak of the spike, not the threshold voltage that opens the channels.

questions.learning_objective: State the threshold voltage, as taught in this course, at which voltage-gated Na+ channels activate.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Action Potential > Sodium Channel Gating

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.16
